newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: UN releases names of staff slain in Rwanda.
newsitem.headline: UN releases names of staff slain in Rwanda.

text.p: The U.N. human rights office on Wednesday released the names of five staff, including a Briton and a Cambodian, murdered on Tuesday in an ambush in Rwanda.

It named the Briton as Graham Turnbull, teamleader for U.N. human rights observers in Cyangugu region where the ambush took place, the Cambodian as Sastra Chim-Chan, who was serving as a U.N. volunteer, and two Rwandans as Jean-Bosco Munyaneza and Aimable Nsensiyumvu.
A fifth victim, the Rwandan driver of the U.N. car who was the only witness to the ambush and who died later in hospital from gunshot wounds, was named as Agripain Ngabo.
The five were killed while visiting the commune of Karengera in Cyangugu, approximately 200 miles (350 km) southwest of Kigali on the Zairean border, in a marked U.N. vehicle.
There were no details on who carried out the ambush. There have been eight violent attacks on expatriates in Rwanda over the past three weeks and none of the attackers have been caught.
U.N. humanitarian sources in Geneva said the U.N. human rights office was likely to come under pressure to pull out its 139 observers from the tiny Central African country to avoid further attacks.

U.N. High Commissioner for Human Rights Jose Ayala Lasso strongly condemned the killings on Tuesday and ordered human rights officers in Rwanda's border regions of Cyangugu, Gisenyi and Kibuye areas to evacuate to Kigali.
It was the first loss of life from an attack in the Human Rights Field Operation in Rwanda, which monitors rights abuses.
The United Nations refugee agency UNHCR said on Tuesday that it too had ordered its expatriate staffers in Rwanda's border regions back to Kigali.
Cyangugu is a heavily militarised and very tense region where Rwanda's Tutsi-dominated army is facing an insurgency by rebels of the Hutu majority operating from neighbouring Burundi.
The predominantly Hutu region also borders Zaire.

Western aid officials in Kigali on Wednesday discussed ways to tighten security for aid workers in response to the growing violence, which has put at risk their work to help Rwanda rebuild from its 1994 genocide.

Marie Van Der Elst, a spokeswoman for the U.N. human rights office in Kigali, said the bodies of British and Cambodian monitors killed in the Tuesday ambush were flown back to the capital from Cyangugu late on Tuesday.
The two corpses were taken to the morgue at Kigali Central Hospital while plans were made for them to be flown out.
Security fears forced monitors in the northwest provinces of Ruhengeri and Gisenyi back to the capital following the killing in cold blood of three Spanish aid workers on January 18.
The government blamed Hutu rebels for their killings but the assailants have yet to be found.
A 61-year-old Canadian missionary was killed by a lone gunman on Sunday while he was giving communion at his parish church in a village 20 km (12 miles) north of Ruhengeri.
